title: Types of Hazards
learningObjectives: Classify hazards into the five main categories
Identify specific hazards within each category
Describe Gulf-specific hazards including heat stress and H2S
Explain why hazard identification is the first step in risk assessment

content.text: Before you can assess risk, you must first identify hazards. Hazards are grouped into five main categories. Understanding these categories ensures you don't miss any hazard during a risk assessment or workplace inspection.

rows: Energy-based hazards that can directly injure the body
Noise, vibration, temperature extremes, radiation, falling objects, electricity
Hazardous substances that can harm through contact, inhalation, or ingestion
Solvents, acids, gases (H2S, CO), dust, asbestos, pesticides
Living organisms or their by-products that cause disease
Bacteria, viruses, mould, insects, rodents, blood-borne pathogens
Work design factors that cause musculoskeletal injury over time
Manual handling, repetitive motion, poor posture, awkward positions
Work organisation factors affecting mental health and wellbeing
Excessive workload, harassment, shift work, job insecurity, isolation

content.text: Physical hazards are the most visible and common in industrial workplaces. They involve various forms of energy that can transfer to the body and cause injury.

items: Noise — Continuous exposure above 85 dB(A) causes permanent hearing loss (NIHL). Common in construction, manufacturing, and drilling
Vibration — Hand-arm vibration from power tools causes HAVS (Hand-Arm Vibration Syndrome). Whole-body vibration from vehicles causes back injuries
Temperature Extremes — Heat causes heat exhaustion and heat stroke; cold causes hypothermia and frostbite
Radiation — Ionising (X-rays, gamma rays) and non-ionising (UV, laser, radiofrequency) radiation
Mechanical — Moving machinery parts, rotating equipment, unguarded blades
Electrical — Shock, burns, arc flash from electrical systems

content.text: HEAT STRESS is the most critical physical hazard in the Gulf. Summer temperatures regularly exceed 45°C with high humidity. Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Human Resources prohibits outdoor work between 12:00 PM and 3:00 PM from June 15 to September 15 each year. UAE enforces similar regulations. All Gulf HSE professionals must be able to explain heat stress controls: acclimatisation, hydration, buddy systems, WBGT monitoring, and emergency response.
Chemical hazards are particularly important in the Gulf's oil & gas sector. Workers can be exposed through inhalation, skin absorption, ingestion, or injection.

items: Gases — H2S, CO, methane, chlorine; many are colourless and odourless at dangerous concentrations
Vapours — Evaporation of liquids like benzene, toluene, solvents
Dusts — Silica dust (causing silicosis), welding fume, asbestos fibres
Liquids — Acids, caustics, oils, pesticides
Fumes — Metal fumes from welding operations

content.text: A colourless, flammable, extremely toxic gas with a characteristic rotten egg smell at low concentrations. At concentrations above 100 ppm, the smell disappears (olfactory fatigue), giving a false sense of safety. At 1000 ppm, death can occur within minutes. H2S is a critical hazard in Gulf oil & gas operations. OEL (Occupational Exposure Limit): 1 ppm (ceiling: 5 ppm in most GCC countries).
Do not trust your nose to detect H2S at dangerous levels. Olfactory fatigue means you stop smelling it just as concentrations become lethal. Always use gas detection equipment.
Biological hazards are often overlooked in industrial HSE but are critical in certain sectors and environments.

items: Healthcare settings — Blood-borne pathogens (HIV, Hepatitis B/C), airborne diseases (TB)
Outdoor construction in Gulf — Insects, scorpions, snakes; risk of MERS-CoV in the Arabian Peninsula
Food processing — Salmonella, E.coli, Listeria
Wastewater — Leptospirosis, Weil's disease
Legionella — Found in poorly maintained cooling towers and water systems; causes Legionnaires' disease

content.text: Ergonomic hazards cause musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) — injuries to muscles, tendons, nerves, and joints. They are the leading cause of work-related ill health in many industries.

items: Manual Handling — Lifting, carrying, pushing, pulling loads incorrectly
Repetitive Movements — Assembly line work, data entry, typing
Awkward Postures — Working in confined spaces, overhead work, twisted positions
Contact Stress — Pressing against hard edges or surfaces repeatedly
Static Loading — Maintaining the same position for extended periods

content.text: The TILE acronym is used for manual handling assessment: Task, Individual, Load, Environment. Use this framework when assessing manual handling risk.
Psychosocial hazards affect mental and emotional health. They are increasingly recognised as major causes of work-related illness, including stress, anxiety, depression, and burnout.

items: Work Demands — Excessive workload, impossible deadlines, insufficient resources
Control — Little autonomy over how work is done
Support — Inadequate support from managers and colleagues
Relationships — Bullying, harassment, discrimination
Role — Role ambiguity or role conflict
Change — Poorly managed organisational change

content.text: Psychosocial hazards are increasingly recognised in Gulf workplaces, particularly for migrant workers who face isolation, heat exposure, financial stress, and communication barriers. ADNOC and Saudi Aramco have wellbeing programmes addressing mental health. As an HSE professional, you should be able to identify and report psychosocial risk factors.
